mcqs.question: What is the defining characteristic of 'unstructured' concurrency, as this topic uses the term?
options: There is no code anywhere that owns tracking whether a spawned task finished, failed, or should be cancelled
It refers to any concurrency model that doesn't use threads
It only applies to single-threaded programs
It means the program uses more than one programming language
mcqs.explanation: Unstructured concurrency's defining problem is the absence of ownership scaffolding — a spawned task with nobody responsible for its completion, failure, or cancellation. It isn't defined by which execution model is used, isn't limited to single-threaded programs, and has nothing to do with language count.

mcqs.question: What is the core rule that defines structured concurrency?
options: A concurrent scope must not exit until every child task it spawned has finished or been explicitly cancelled
Every task must run on its own dedicated thread
Tasks must be spawned in alphabetical order by name
A program may only spawn one concurrent task at a time
mcqs.explanation: This single rule — a scope's exit gated on all its children's completion or cancellation — is structured concurrency's entire foundation, converting task-lifetime tracking from a discipline into a structural guarantee. It says nothing about thread-per-task, spawn ordering, or limiting concurrent task counts.

mcqs.question: In a structured concurrency scope with three child tasks, the parent scope is cancelled. What happens to the children by default?
options: Nothing — each child continues running until it finishes on its own
Only the first child spawned is cancelled
All three children are automatically cancelled as well, with no manual per-task bookkeeping required
The children are paused indefinitely rather than cancelled
mcqs.explanation: Because each child is owned by the parent scope, cancelling the parent automatically propagates cancellation to every child — this is exactly the guarantee that fixes manually-tracked, easy-to-miss cancellation in unstructured code. Children aren't left running, aren't cancelled selectively by spawn order, and aren't merely paused.

mcqs.question: An unawaited promise throws an exception deep inside a 'fire and forget' background task. What typically happens to that exception in unstructured code?
options: It automatically triggers a full program crash
It is silently swallowed unless something explicitly attached an error handler to that specific task
It is automatically logged by the language runtime
It propagates synchronously to whatever code line happens to execute next
mcqs.explanation: With nothing watching an unawaited, detached task, its exception has nowhere defined to go and is silently lost unless explicit handling was attached — this exact problem is what a structured scope fixes by guaranteeing something is always watching. It doesn't crash the whole program by default, isn't auto-logged, and doesn't propagate synchronously to unrelated code.

mcqs.question: A client disconnects, cancelling a request, but the server keeps doing background work related to that request for 30 more seconds. What's the most likely structural cause?
options: The server's garbage collector is running a full collection cycle
A background task was spawned as a 'fire and forget' operation, never made a child of the request's own scope, so the request's cancellation had no way to reach it
The network connection is still technically open at the TCP level
The CPU is simply too slow to process the cancellation in time
mcqs.explanation: This is the classic structured-concurrency failure mode: an orphaned background task with no owning scope has no cancellation signal reaching it, so it keeps running regardless of whether the request that spawned it still cares about the result. GC cycles, raw connection state, and CPU speed aren't the structural cause of this specific pattern.

mcqs.question: What capability does unstructured futures/promises retain that structured concurrency deliberately gives up by default?
options: The ability to run more than one task at a time
The ability to accidentally or deliberately detach a task from any owning scope entirely
The ability to return a value from an asynchronous operation
The ability to run on multiple CPU cores
mcqs.explanation: Unstructured code allows a task to be detached from any owner, whether intentionally or by accident; structured concurrency trades that flexibility away so every task is always accounted for by some scope. Neither model is restricted in running multiple tasks, returning values, or using multiple cores.
